passage:
Monday. Damini watched Ms Varghese hand back the spelling test. “Kabir got six right, up from two,” the teacher said. “That is real work.” Kabir sat up straight.
Wednesday. A boy copied the way Lalremsiami counted on fingers under the desk, and a few children giggled. The teacher put down her chalk. “In this room nobody laughs at how somebody works things out. Show us, Lalremsiami, and we'll watch.” Lalremsiami counted again, openly this time, and got the sum right. The giggling boy went red and looked at his desk.
Friday. Another child got a sum wrong. Damini heard the girl next to her whisper, “Good try, look, you're nearly there.” The teacher, at the board, did not turn around, but she smiled.

qa.q: On which day did the teacher stop the giggling?
qa.a: On Wednesday the teacher stopped the giggling after a boy copied how Lalremsiami counted on fingers.

qa.q: How might Lalremsiami have felt when the teacher said, “Show us, Lalremsiami, and we'll watch”?
qa.a: Lalremsiami probably felt protected but still exposed, since Lalremsiami counted again in front of everyone after being mocked, and the room then watched.

qa.q: What small choice by the teacher on Wednesday did the most to change the room?
qa.a: Stopping the mockery straight away, and then asking Lalremsiami to show the method, so that the child who was laughed at was heard and not shamed further.

qa.q: What might Damini have noticed about how the teacher's habits spread by Friday?
qa.a: Damini noticed that a girl now whispered, “Good try,” to the child beside her after a wrong sum, the same effort-praising tone the teacher used, which shows children copy what the teacher does.

grounding: A teacher who praises effort, stops mockery quickly and applies the same rules to everyone sets a climate that children copy, seen by a pupil.

passage: “Come here, my little Zoya, and I'll tell you about Mr Anand,” said Nani Salma. “When I was ten, our teacher was Mr Anand, and our class had a girl called Meena who read very slowly. One day a boy began copying her, and the room laughed. Mr Anand did not shout. He walked to the back, stood beside Meena's desk and said, 'In this room everyone gets the time they need. Meena, please begin again.' We waited. Meena finished, red in the face, and he said, 'Thank you. Well read.' Next day my bench-mate Hafsa told a shy boy, 'Take your time.' I heard myself say it too. We had copied him without knowing.”

qa.q: Where did Mr Anand stand when he spoke to the class about Meena?
qa.a: Mr Anand stood beside Meena's desk at the back of the room.

qa.q: What might Meena have felt while the class waited for her to finish?
qa.a: Meena probably felt nervous and exposed but also supported, since Meena finished red in the face and was thanked for reading well.

qa.q: What could a teacher do today when a child is mocked for reading slowly?
qa.a: A teacher could stop it calmly, stand near the child, give the child time to read and thank them for it, as Mr Anand did.

qa.q: How might the boy who copied Meena have felt when the teacher spoke?
qa.a: The boy may have felt caught and ashamed, since the room stopped laughing and the teacher's calm words made the copying look unwelcome.

grounding: An elder remembers a teacher who stopped mockery calmly and treated everyone the same, and how the children copied his manner.

passage: The drilling next door started at nine, and Mrs Mathew had to raise her voice over it. Joseph sat by the window and watched her the way he always did. When Aadhya read her essay aloud and mixed up 'there' and 'their', Kevin snorted. Mrs Mathew stopped the whole class, drill and all. 'Kevin, in this room we don't laugh at mistakes. You'll get the same kindness when you try.' Then, to Aadhya, 'Your idea about the stray dog was the best part. Carry on.' Joseph noticed she used the same calm voice for Kevin as for everyone. Later, when the drill made Priti lose her place and someone began to giggle, Joseph heard himself say, 'We don't laugh at that.'

qa.q: What did Aadhya mix up in her essay?
qa.a: 'There' and 'their'.

qa.q: What was Joseph noticing and feeling as he watched Mrs Mathew?
qa.a: Joseph was paying close attention and seemed reassured and impressed that she used the same calm voice for Kevin as for everyone.

qa.q: What in Mrs Mathew's response is worth copying?
qa.a: She stopped the mocking at once, stayed calm and fair, and praised the strongest part of Aadhya's work.

qa.q: What might Mrs Mathew be hoping for when she stops the class, even with the drill going?
qa.a: She likely wants every child to feel safe making mistakes, knowing that if one snort passes, others will copy it.

grounding: A child watches a teacher stop mockery quickly and fairly on a noisy day, and then copies her in class.

passage: In Class 4C at a Pune municipal school, Irfan watched Usha ma'am's face more than the blackboard. He could tell a lot from it. When Karan, the class monitor, talked during the test, she took his paper away for a minute, exactly as she had done with Irfan's bench-mate Sunny the day before. Same rule. When Sunny finished a sum after three wrong tries, she tapped his notebook and said, 'Three tries! That's how brains grow.' Irfan saw Sunny sit up straighter. And when two girls rolled their eyes at a new student's accent, ma'am only said, 'Eyes to the board,' very quietly, and it stopped. By Friday, Irfan noticed the whole class saying 'Three tries!' to each other whenever someone got stuck.

qa.q: What did Usha ma'am do when Karan talked during the test?
qa.a: She took his paper away for a minute, exactly as she had done with Sunny the day before.

qa.q: Why does Irfan watch Usha ma'am's face so closely?
qa.a: He seems curious and a little cautious, reading her small reactions to learn what is safe and fair in class.

qa.q: What small habit of Usha ma'am's could another teacher use?
qa.a: Praising effort out loud, like 'Three tries!', and applying the same rule to the monitor as to everyone else.

qa.q: How might Usha ma'am see the class copying 'Three tries!' by Friday?
qa.a: She would likely feel pleased and encouraged, seeing that her small reactions are shaping how the children treat each other.

grounding: A child notices how a teacher's fair rules and praise for effort set a climate the class begins to copy.

passage:
'How's the new teacher?' Binita asked, peeling an orange at the kitchen table.
'Different,' said Bidisha, dropping her bag. 'Today Ritwik called Poulomi "slowpoke", and Sir stopped the whole lesson.'
'Did he shout?'
'No. He just said, "Ritwik, that's not how we speak in here," and waited till Ritwik said sorry. Then he carried on like nothing happened.'
'Hmm. Our old teacher would have laughed.'
'I know! And he checks everyone's homework the same way, even the topper's. When Poulomi got a sum wrong later, he said, "Good try, check step two." She actually smiled.'
Binita handed over a piece of orange. 'You like him.'
'I don't know yet,' Bidisha said. 'But nobody laughed at Poulomi after that. Not even at lunch.'

qa.q: What did Ritwik call Poulomi?
qa.a: 'Slowpoke'.

qa.q: What does Bidisha's 'I don't know yet' suggest?
qa.a: Bidisha feels curious and cautiously hopeful, still watching the new teacher before fully trusting him.

qa.q: What did Sir's response teach the class?
qa.a: That mocking stops at once and everyone follows the same rules, which is why nobody laughed at Poulomi afterwards, not even at lunch.

qa.q: Why might Sir carry on 'like nothing happened' after the apology?
qa.a: He likely wants to stop the mocking without making a big scene, so Ritwik isn't humiliated and the class sees the rule matters.

grounding: A child describes at home how a new teacher's calm, equal response to mockery changed how classmates behave.

passage: I'm Nirmala, and when I was in Class 4, I watched Payal Miss more than the blackboard. On the first day, Rohit laughed when Gita read "island" as "is-land". Miss didn't shout. She only said, "In this room we don't laugh at reading," and waited until Rohit said sorry. Then she told Gita, "You tried the hard word first. Good." Even Arun, whose mother taught next door, had to wait in the lunch line like everyone. After a while I noticed we were copying her. When Gita got stuck again in December, it was Rohit who whispered the sound. I think all of us were watching Miss's eyebrows, to learn what was allowed.

qa.q: How did Gita read the word "island"?
qa.a: Gita read "island" as "is-land".

qa.q: What does Nirmala's habit of watching Payal Miss's eyebrows suggest?
qa.a: Nirmala felt curious and a little cautious, reading the teacher's small reactions to learn what was safe in the room.

qa.q: Which of Payal Miss's choices set the tone, and why did it work?
qa.a: She stopped the laughing calmly, praised Gita's effort, and made Arun follow the same rules, so the class learned fairness by watching her.

qa.q: What is it like for Gita when Rohit whispers the sound in December?
qa.a: Gita gets help instead of mockery from the same classmate who once laughed, which shows the class had copied the teacher's way.

grounding: Nirmala, as a watching classmate, sees how a teacher who stops mockery, praises effort and applies the same rules sets a climate children copy.
